scenarios.setup: A battery, a variable resistor, and an ammeter connected in a simple loop.

tasks.prompt: Double the voltage from 2V to 4V. Predict what happens to the current.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Current doubles. According to Ohm's Law (V = IR), current is directly proportional to voltage when resistance is constant.

tasks.prompt: Keep the voltage at 4V. Double the resistance. Predict what happens to the current.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Current halves. Current is inversely proportional to resistance.
tasks.anomalyExplanation: Many students intuitively think 'more resistance means more current'. Ohm's Law shows the opposite: I = V/R. Higher resistance means lower current for the same voltage.

scenarios.setup: Two identical bulbs, a battery, and a switch. A toggle to wire them in series or parallel.

tasks.prompt: Wire the bulbs in SERIES. Predict their brightness compared to a single bulb.
predictionOptions: Both will be dimmer than a single bulb
Both will be brighter than a single bulb
tasks.expectedOutcome: Both will be dimmer. In series, the voltage is shared between the bulbs, so each gets less voltage.

tasks.prompt: In the SERIES circuit, unscrew one bulb. Predict what happens to the other bulb.
tasks.expectedOutcome: The other bulb goes out. In a series circuit, there is only one path for current. Breaking the circuit anywhere stops the flow everywhere.
tasks.anomalyExplanation: In a parallel circuit, removing one bulb does not affect the other because each has its own path to the battery. This is a critical difference.

scenarios.setup: A thin fuse wire in a circuit with a variable voltage source.

tasks.prompt: Slowly increase the voltage. Predict what will happen to the fuse wire.
tasks.expectedOutcome: It will glow and melt. The heating effect of current (H = I²Rt) causes the wire to heat up. If the current is too high, the wire melts, breaking the circuit.
